boundary: Zend's allocator: temporal defects in PHP 5.0.0 whose freed block never reaches libc, because _efree parks it in AG(cache) and a later emalloc hands the same bytes to the next object
title: Thirty temporal defects live in PHP 5.0.0 that a detector interposing at malloc cannot see, because the release stops at the nested allocator
live_in_pin_note: Liveness is measured at the pin, not inferred from a date: every case's trigger was run on a build of php-5.0.0 from the museum tarball (sha256 5783e0c0ba94f165633a565fe73a83e59cf17b6880ef95fa8f936dc6301d6919) and reported under ASan, and the defective construct is quoted from the pin's own source in each PROVENANCE.md. What is NOT established in this tree is the upstream side of the pair: php-src's history is not on this host, so each fix is cited by hash and its hunk is not quoted.
note: THE SPLIT BETWEEN THIS CORPUS AND ITS SIBLING IS MEASURED, NOT ARGUED. Both hold temporal defects of the same release; what separates them is one reading. Each trigger was run twice on this host, on two builds of the same source that differ only in two defines in Zend/zend_alloc.c: the source corpus's detector build (ZEND_DISABLE_MEMORY_CACHE 1, REAL_SIZE unrounded), where every efree reaches free() and ASan sees every lifetime end, and the allocator AS SHIPPED. All thirty cases here keep a temporal report on the first and lose it on the second -- 21 go completely silent (exit 0), 7 degrade to a SEGV ASan cannot attribute to a heap event, one to EXIT:255 and one to a heap-buffer-overflow in an unrelated region. The sibling corpus's twenty-six keep it on both. That is the whole claim this corpus exists to carry: detector blindness is a property of WHERE a detector interposes, not of how strong it is, and both ASan and CHERI interpose below the nested allocator. The mechanism is in the source, not inferred: _efree pushes a block whose payload is at most 80 bytes onto AG(cache) and returns (Zend/zend_alloc.c:270-282, MAX_CACHED_MEMORY 11 over an 8-byte index), so free() is never called and the libc block stays live and in bounds for the whole window. Size alone does not decide it -- the per-class cache holds 256 entries and _erealloc never uses the cache at all -- which is why the split comes from the run and not from a size rule. CASE SELECTION: the two corpora together are 56 of the source corpus's 185 cases. Only temporal defects were taken (CWE-416, CWE-415, CWE-590, plus two the source corpus labels by symptom -- CWE-822 and CWE-476 -- whose recorded root cause is a use after free); leaks, refcount-only defects, reference bindings, uninitialised reads, type confusions, null dereferences and every spatial class were left out. Five stack-use-after-return cases (CWE-562) are temporal but cross neither allocator and are left out too. Six more were dropped because neither build produced a temporal verdict for them (CRASH-026, 034, 064, 071, 139) or because the trigger needs a loopback listener this host does not provide (CRASH-092). THE ARMS. virtual-malloc is php-real-stock, PHP_CAP_MODE=0: the seam image with nothing revoked, so the only protection is musl mallocng's own per-object bounds and its retirement of a lifetime at free -- the baseline a catch is measured against, and the arm this corpus predicts will read MISSED. virtual-nested-pools is php-real-exact, PHP_CAP_MODE=7: every emalloc block a CDERIVE child bounded at the caller's own size and CREVOKEd at efree, which is the only arm that sees a release Zend's cache absorbs. cheribsd-revocation is stock CheriBSD purecap, which interposes where mallocng does and is predicted to read like virtual-malloc. Four cases need bundled extensions the app port does not build (--disable-all), and two need a writable /tmp; each says so in its own fidelity.
